newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Perry says NATO rift has not "soured" U.S.-French ties.
newsitem.headline: Perry says NATO rift has not "soured" U.S.-French ties.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Monday that broad U.S.-French relations had not been soured by a bitter dispute over NATO reorganization, but insisted Washington would not bow to French demands to give up command of the alliance's southern flank.

"It is not an issue which has soured or affected our other relations with the French," Perry said. "It is not a personal issue. I still have excellent working and personal relationships with Minister Millon. I expect to meet and talk with him in the next day or two."

He spoke to reporters after arriving in Brussels for two days of talks with NATO defence ministers, including France's Charles Millon, on issues ranging from Bosnia peacekeeping to whether a U.S. officer will continue to command southern NATO forces based in Naples.
France is demanding that Washington surrender that traditional U.S. post to a European officer.
But the United States has refused to do so, saying the American military has a preponderance of forces in the region, including the powerful U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean.
"Our position, I think, has been umambigious and unchangeable on that point and I do not expect that position to change," Perry said in response to questions.

"I do not expect to resolve that issue at this meeting, but I am confident we will find a solution to this problem. It is just too important for the United States, for France, for NATO to find a solution."

Despite Perry's comments about overall U.S. French relations, relations have cooled sufficiently for the United States to accuse French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette of intentionally snubbing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher during a tribute to Christopher by fellow foreign ministers here last week.
French officials said de Charette had left the meeting unaware that a toast was to be made to Christopher and denied that the move was an intentional snub.
On another subject, Perry said on Monday the international community must keep pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to recognise an election victory by opposition parties in his country.

The secretary was asked by reporters about demonstrations by hundreds of thousands of Serbs in Belgrade in the past month and opposition coalition charges that Milosevic's ruling socialists cheated it out of victory in large Serbian cities, including Belgrade, during the November 17 local elections.
"The United States view on that has been stated pretty clearly by the State Department," Perry said.
"We believe that these election results should be honoured," he said. "Subverting democratic election processes is an action which the United States cannot support."
Perry, 69, has resigned after three years at the Pentagon and is expected to be succeeded in early February by moderate Republican U.S. Senator William Cohen of Maine.

Perry flew to Brussels from Germany, where he met U.S. troops from the First Armoured Division who have been serving in Bosnia for the past year as part of a NATO-led international peace implementation force (IFOR) of 50,000 troops.

That force will be replaced beginning on December 20 by a smaller NATO-led "stabilisation" force (SFOR) of some 30,000 troops -- 8,500 of them Americans -- which will remain in Bosnia until mid-1998 to oversee peace while international organisations move to rebuild the country.

In addition to meeting fellow NATO defence ministers over the next two days, Perry will also hold talks with Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Wednesday in Washington's continuing move to establish closer bilateral ties with Moscow and improve Russian cooperation with the Atlantic alliance.
